entry.title: Introducing the Comment Management Dashboard in SAP Analytics Cloud: Full Control Over Your Comments
entry.content:
If you are Planner or Analyst in SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC), you know how valuable Data Point Comments are for capturing qualitative context alongside your numbers. But as comment volumes grow across users, versions, and models, they become increasingly difficult to govern. In this blog, I walk through the new Comment Management Dashboard — a purpose-built admin tool that gives you full visibility and control over comments across your entire SAC tenant.

What is a Data Point Comment in SAP Analytics Cloud(SAC)?

A Data Point Comment is an annotation tied directly to a specific data cell (or data point) within an SAC table and comment widget.Users can target an exact intersection of dimensions and measures—such as a specific product line's sales figure for a specific month in a specific region.

Unlike comments embedded purely within the story layout, Data Point Comments are stored at the Model level rather than the Story level. This architectural distinction makes them immensely powerful.

Key Characteristics & Benefits of Data Point Comments

  • Model-Level Persistence: Because data point comments live within the underlying data model, any new story or analytical application built on that same model will automatically inherit and display these comments if the data context matches.
  • Context-Aware: Comments track the precise filter, Data authorization and dimension context of the cell. If data values change or refresh, the comment retains its historical context (often snapshotting the original value when the comment was created).
  • Cross-Platform Synergy: Data point comments seamlessly integrate beyond SAC stories. For instance, users working in the SAP Analytics Cloud add-in for Microsoft Excel can view, create, and sync these exact same cell-level comments natively in their spreadsheets.
  • Collaboration and Threads: Users can reply to existing comments to build a discussion thread, ensuring that decision-makers have a clear audit trail of why a number looks the way it does.

Comment Administration challenges

While Data Point Comments are essential for adding qualitative context to planning figures, managing them in real-world, enterprise-scale SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC) environments introduces major visibility and administration challenges

The Comment Discovery Challenge

Data point comments are added by multiple users across various tables and stories within SAC. Because every cell's unique data point is formed by a specific combination of filters, Data Access Control (DAC), and table coordinates, it is practically impossible to view or locate all comments associated with a model inside a standard SAC table.

Users frequently lose track of comments when:

  • Table Filter Values Change: Filters applied to a story or table hide cells where comments were previously added.
  • Dimension Members are Modified: Adding or deleting dimension members shifts or breaks the context.
  • Data Authorization (DAC) Changes: Security role updates change what data a user can see, hiding previously visible comments.
  • Table Coordinates Change: Row or column layout adjustments alter the visual location of commented cells.

Administrative & Lifecycle Management Bottlenecks

Beyond locating comments, Comment administrators face severe limitations when performing routine maintenance and governance operations:

  • Targeted Deletions: Deleting all comments tied to a specific Account Member or a specific Model Version is extremely difficult.
  • Holistic Visibility & Auditing: There is no quick way to get an enterprise-wide overview of:
    • All comments associated with a specific version or account member.
    • Recent activity (e.g., all comments added in the last week or month).
  • Version Operations: Copying comments seamlessly from one planning version to another or exporting comments tied to a specific version for offline auditing/reporting is challenging.
  • Previewing Comments: Reviewing comment threads in bulk without navigating to individual story widgets is cumbersome.

The Solution: Introducing the Comment Management Dashboard

To overcome these operational and administrative pain points, we developed the Comment Management Dashboard.

Designed specifically for comment administrators and privileged users, this central admin tool provides complete visibility and control over Data Point and Dimension Comments across an entire SAC tenant. It transforms unmanageable, scattered cell annotations into a structured, audit-ready asset.

Key Workflows Enabled by the Dashboard

The Comment Management Dashboard supports several critical administrative workflows:

  • Model Inventory: Instantly list all models within the tenant that contain comments.
  • Model-Level Statistics: Access an executive overview of comment metrics and activity statistics aggregated at the model level.
  • Centralized Comment Preview: Preview comments associated with a model directly from a unified interface without opening individual stories.
  • Bulk Copy Comments: Copy comments across versions or models in bulk to streamline planning cycles.
  • Bulk Delete Comments: Efficiently clean up outdated or redundant comments in bulk across specific dimensions, accounts, or versions.
  • CSV Export: Export all comments from a model directly into a CSV file for offline analysis, archiving, or auditing purposes.

Detailed Breakdown of Key Capabilities

Privileges and settings

  • To get Access to Comment Management dashboard
    • User need Read and Manage comments privileges at the role level to view Comment Management Dashboard
  • To view models in the Comment Management Dashboard
    • User need Read comment and Maintain model privileges at the model level and Read and maintain at the role level to view the models in the comment management dashboard.
  • To delete comment from a model
    • User need Delete comments privileges at the role and model level to delete comments from model or its versions.
  • To Export comment from a model
    • Tenant Admin need to enable configuration “Allow Comment Export” under administration – System configuration to enable export comment from a model.

Model Discovery & Statistics Overview

    • Once user has necessary privileges, they will be able to view comment management in the left panel and on click of it they will get inside the Comment management dashboard where they can see list of models accessible to them and their related comment statistic per model such as
      • Number of Comments thread
      • Number of datapoint comments
      • Number of dimension comments
      • Total number of Comments
      • Comment Statistic at the version level
        • List all versions in model
        • Number of comment and dimension comment per version

Comment Management Dashboard — Model Statistics Overview

 

Comment Management Dashboard — Version Statistics Overview

 

Centralized Comment Preview & Filtering

    • User can select any of the model and then preview all comments associated with the model.

Preview comments associated with model

    • User will also have an option to filter and preview comments, they can filter on comments properties and the model attributes such as
      • Comment properties 
        • Comment/Thread creation date
        • Comment Modified date
        • Comment/Thread Owner
      • Dimension
      • Account
      • Measures

 

Filter option

Bulk Delete

    • Bulk deletion can be performed from multiple locations within the dashboard
      • User can perform bulk delete of all comments (dimension and datapoint comments) at the model and this can be done from the main dashboard page where the models are listed
      • User can perform bulk delete of all comments associated with version and this can be done from the version listing page for a model
      • User can also perform selectively delete from the comment preview page.

Delete all comment from a model

 

Delete all comment from a Version

Bulk Copy comment

    • User can perform bulk copy of comment and this gives users the flexibility to perform copy operations such as
      • Copy all Comment from one version to another version
      • Copy comment from one dimension member to another dimension member such as 
        • Copy from date dimension member, example Year 2025 to 2026
        • Copy comment from Generic dimension member product X to product Y
      • Copy selected comments using filter

Copy comment – rule and filter options

Comment Export

    • User can perform Export comment. To enable this feature, a Tenant Admin must activate the "Allow Comment Export" setting under Administration → System Configuration. Once this is done they will be able to
      • Export all comments from the comment preview page
      • Export all, minus few comments from the preview page
    • They can filter comments to preview and same filtered comment they can export
    • In the export they will have additional column which will contain the dimension on which filter is applied

Conclusion

The Comment Management Dashboard transforms a previously scattered, difficult-to-govern comments into a structured, audit-ready capability. Whether you are a planning or Analyst administrator managing thousands of comments across model versions, or who needs to clean up legacy comments before a new planning cycle, this dashboard gives you the tools to do it efficiently and reliably.

Have you tried the Comment Management Dashboard? Share your experience or questions in the comments below.

entry.title: From Datasphere to SAC: When a Model Becomes a Business Answer
entry.content:
After working through the BW-to-Datasphere and S/4HANA-to-Datasphere sides of an analytics project, I started looking at the final part of the landscape a little differently.

We had spent time understanding the existing reporting logic, bringing data into Datasphere, building the required views, defining measures, and organizing the data into analytical models. Eventually, all that work had to reach SAP Analytics Cloud. This is where things get interesting.

A model can be activated successfully. The measures can return the expected values. The joins can work as intended. You can open the model, run your queries, and convince yourself that the development is moving in the right direction.

Then you build the SAC story.

A KPI shows an unexpected number. A filter changes the result in a way you didn't anticipate. A chart works in one context but behaves differently when the same data is consumed somewhere else. And suddenly, the problem doesn't look like a modeling problem anymore.

At least, not at first.

During my work with Datasphere and SAC, I started realizing that the last part of the analytics landscape deserves just as much attention as everything that happens before it. Because building a model and making that model useful to the business are two very different things.

The model was ready. Was the reporting ready?

In one of our project scenarios, we were working with financial and sales reporting requirements that needed to be exposed through SAC.

The Datasphere side involved the usual layers: raw data, harmonization views, reporting views, and analytical models. On the SAC side, the requirement was to turn those models into something business users could actually work with.

We were not building a single chart and calling it done.

The story needed to support different perspectives of the business: an executive overview, regional performance, customer analysis, and finance. That meant dealing with KPIs, charts, tables, filters, and different levels of detail. The obvious approach would have been to finish the Datasphere models first and then start building the story.

But I found that the relationship between the two is more iterative than that.

While building the SAC story, questions started coming up that were not obvious when looking at the model in isolation.

Does this measure represent the number the business expects to see?
Should this filter affect every widget on the page?
Should this calculation be reusable across multiple stories, or does it only make sense in one particular visualization?
Does the user need the aggregated number, or do they need to understand what is contributing to it?

These questions influence the modeling decisions just as much as they influence the story design, and that is where I started seeing SAC as more than the final presentation layer. It becomes the place where the quality of the entire analytical design is tested.

A KPI is a small number with a lot of responsibility

One thing I have come to appreciate is how much responsibility we place on a KPI card.

A chart gives the user some context. A table lets them inspect the underlying values. But a KPI often presents a single number and expects the user to trust it immediately.

Imagine an executive opening a sales dashboard.

The first thing they see is total sales. Below that, they see regional performance, customer contribution, and a breakdown of financial metrics. If the total is incorrect, the entire dashboard loses credibility. But the interesting part is that the number can be wrong for several different reasons.

The source data may be incomplete. The Datasphere model may aggregate the data differently than expected. A filter may be applied incorrectly. A measure may have the wrong semantic definition. Or the SAC widget may be consuming a different model or connection than the developer assumes.

From the user's perspective, all of these problems look the same. 

The dashboard is showing the wrong number.

From the developer's perspective, they are completely different problems. This is why I prefer to validate a KPI at the model level before spending time polishing its appearance in SAC. If the analytical model returns the wrong result, changing the formatting, chart type, or story layout will not solve the underlying problem. And if the model returns the correct result but the SAC widget does not, the investigation needs to move toward the consumption layer.

The important thing is to identify where the result changes, rather than assuming that the layer where the problem becomes visible is the layer where it originated.

Filters are where a simple dashboard can become complicated

Another part of SAC development that deserves more attention is filter behavior.

In our reporting work, the story needed to support filters such as Year, Period, Region, Product Group, Sales Organization, and GL Account.

Individually, these are straightforward requirements. The complexity appears when they start interacting with different charts, tables, and KPIs.

Consider a user selecting a particular region. They expect the sales KPI, regional chart, customer table, and other relevant widgets to reflect that selection consistently.

But not every widget necessarily uses the same model or has the same dimensional context.

A filter that makes sense for one model may not be available in another. Two models may represent the same business concept differently. A dimension may be present in one analytical model but absent from another.

This is where a dashboard that looks correct during development can become confusing for the user. The issue is not necessarily that the filter is broken. It may be that the underlying models do not support the same interpretation of that filter. For me, this reinforced the importance of thinking about filters while designing the Datasphere models, not just when configuring the SAC story.

Before adding a global filter, I would want to understand which models it needs to affect, whether the relevant dimensions are aligned, and what the expected behavior should be for every widget.

A filter is not simply a control on the screen. It represents a business expectation about how the data should respond.

Then there is the question of where a calculation belongs

This connects directly to the first article in this series, where I discussed translating existing BW reporting logic into Datasphere.

During that work, one question kept coming back: should a particular calculation live in Datasphere or in SAC?

I think this becomes much easier to answer when we stop looking at the calculation itself and start looking at how it will be used. 

Suppose we have a financial measure that needs a particular sign convention.

If that convention represents a reusable business rule, implementing it in the appropriate Datasphere modeling layer can make the result consistent for multiple consumers.

If we instead reproduce the same calculation independently in several SAC stories, we introduce more places where the logic can diverge.

Now consider a calculation that exists purely to support a particular chart or a presentation-specific comparison. That may be better handled in SAC, depending on the requirement and the capabilities involved. 

The point is not that every calculation belongs in Datasphere. It is that we should know why a calculation exists before deciding where to implement it.

I have found this question useful:

If another report needs the same business result tomorrow, should it have to recreate this logic?

If the answer is no, that is a good reason to investigate whether the logic belongs in a reusable model.

This decision affects maintainability, consistency, and how much work is required when the reporting requirement changes.

When a working SAC story is not the end of the story

One of the more interesting issues I encountered was outside the normal SAC story development process.

We were exploring the use of SAC KPI tiles in SAP Build Work Zone. The requirement was to make analytical information available through the Work Zone experience, rather than requiring users to navigate into the SAC story every time they wanted to see a KPI.

The important detail was that the SAC story was using a live connection to a Datasphere analytical model. The story itself could load the Datasphere data correctly.

However, when the same type of KPI was consumed through a Work Zone tile, the request failed with a FAILED_TO_FETCH_DATA error. What made this particularly interesting was that the behavior differed depending on the model type.

KPI tiles using SAC-based acquired models worked, while the equivalent approach using live Datasphere models did not behave the same way.

At that point, it would have been easy to keep changing the Datasphere model or rebuilding the SAC chart. But the fact that the story itself could retrieve the data suggested that we needed to investigate the consumption path as well. The question was no longer simply whether the model worked. It was whether the model and its live connection were supported in the context in which we were trying to consume them.

We investigated the data-fetching path and the relevant connection behavior, and the issue also raised questions about the limitations of the integration between the two environments. I wouldn't describe this as a solved problem. The important lesson was what it revealed about the architecture.

A model working in SAC does not automatically mean every way of embedding or consuming that model will work.

That distinction matters when designing analytics for more than one entry point.

A story, a KPI tile, and an embedded analytical experience may all appear to be displaying the same information, but they can involve different consumption mechanisms and constraints.

Those differences need to be considered during solution design, not discovered after the dashboard has already been built.

Sometimes the problem is not the model or the story. It is the environment.

The Work Zone investigation also connected to another challenge we were dealing with: the SAC and Datasphere tenants were operating in different regions.

The Datasphere tenant was in US21, while the SAC tenant was in US20.

This became relevant when investigating the proposed live connectivity approach. It introduced a dependency that could not be resolved simply by changing a measure or adjusting a chart. The model could be valid. The story could be valid. Yet the intended integration still depended on the connection architecture and the constraints of the environments involved.

We had to consider the tenant setup and discuss the approach internally and with the client while working through the support guidance.

This was a useful reminder that analytics architecture does not stop at the boundary of a Datasphere space or an SAC story. The connection between those environments is part of the solution too. I think this is particularly important when planning live analytics, embedded scenarios, and integrations across multiple SAP services.

Before committing to an approach, I would want to validate the actual connectivity path and the intended consumption scenario, not just confirm that a connection can be created. A connection being available is one thing. The complete reporting experience working as expected is another.

What I now look at when a chart does not behave as expected

These experiences have changed how I approach troubleshooting in SAC.

Earlier in the process, it is tempting to start with the widget itself. Change the measure, change the aggregation, adjust the filter, or try a different chart. Sometimes that is exactly where the problem is.

But I find it more useful to work backwards from the result.

If a KPI is showing zero, I want to know whether the analytical model also returns zero.

If a filter produces an unexpected result, I want to know whether the model contains the necessary dimension and whether the filter is reaching the intended widgets.

If a story works but a Work Zone tile fails, I want to understand how that tile retrieves the data and whether the connection scenario is supported.

The troubleshooting path depends on the symptom, but the underlying approach is the same.

Start with what the user sees. Identify the layer responsible for producing that result. Then verify the assumptions at that layer before changing anything. That approach helps distinguish between a data problem, a modeling problem, a story configuration problem, and a platform integration problem.

It also avoids a common trap in analytics development: changing something that appears related to the symptom without establishing that it caused the issue.

The final mile is where the business judges the entire landscape

Looking back at the three stages of this analytics journey, I see them as closely connected.

In the first stage, we worked on understanding and translating the existing BW reporting logic.

In the second, we dealt with the challenges of bringing S/4HANA data into Datasphere and making sure it was technically, structurally, and semantically suitable for reporting.

In the final stage, we had to turn those models into an analytical experience that the business could use and trust.

Each stage has its own problems, but the final stage brings the earlier decisions together. 
A beautifully designed SAC story cannot compensate for incorrect business logic. 
A correct Datasphere model does not guarantee that every filter, widget, or integration will behave as expected.

And a successful connection does not, by itself, guarantee a successful reporting experience.

For me, this is the part of analytics development that is easy to underestimate. The final charts are visible, so they naturally receive a lot of attention. But what makes those charts trustworthy is everything behind them, together with the decisions made when connecting the model to the user experience.

The goal is not simply to get data onto a screen.

It is to make sure the number on that screen means what the business thinks it means, and that users can access it in the context where they need it.

That is when the analytics landscape starts delivering its real value.

Because ultimately, the model is the foundation, the chart is the interface, and the business decision is the outcome.

entry.title: How to run SAC Pull integration Job from SAP Analytics Cloud Multi Action using API_FINPLANPULLJOB
entry.content:
Introduction

The purpose of this post is to introduce a new service API_FINPLANPULLJOB that was recently included into Communication Scenario SAP_COM_0087 of SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud. This service provides a convenient and tailored mechanism for planner to start integration jobs between SAP Analytics Cloud and SAP S/4HANA Cloud on the direction to S/4HANA by simple click directly from SAC Story using Multi Action.

It provides an alternative, but more direct way to start integration compared to manual start from S/4HANA Fiori application "Schedule Financial Plan Data Jobs". 

The new service is an alternative (so far only for Cloud customers) to the old approach of triggering integration jobs with generic service BC_EXT_APPJOB_MANAGEMENT as it was previously described in the Blog post.

The new service is supporting target types of ACDOCP, FINSSKF, ACCOSTRATE and CCFCTR.

To get the scenario working, some configuration steps are required: starting with configuring users on SAP S/4HANA side, followed by creating HTTP API connection on SAP Analytics Cloud side, and, finally, configuring Multi Action in SAC Story.

In this scenario it is important to understand that three types of S/4HANA users are involved in the process:
    - Communication user;
    - Business user for posting plan data ("posting" user);
    - Business user for monitoring application jobs and application logs ("monitoring" user).

A communication user is only used to call the needed S/4HANA inbound service (API_FINPLANPULLJOB) from SAC tenant, whereas the "posting" user is bearing all necessary authorizations for integrating data to respective target tables, for example, ACDOCP. Even though the whole process is triggered by SAC using the communication user, the actual integration Job gets started on behalf of "posting" user. After the job is finished, it collects application logs in the system. This log "belongs" to the communication user and by-default for security reasons is not available for reading by any other S/4HANA user. Therefore, we need a third type of user – a "monitoring user" which has extra authorization to see application logs of other S/4HANA users, i.e. to read logs created by communication user. The "posting" and "monitoring" can technically be the same S/4HANA user.

The following block-diagram provides a conceptual view on service architecture:

The following flow diagram describes an example of typical process, starting from pressing "Multi Action Starter" button in your Story, invoking all three types of endpoints, until a final message toast is displayed on the screen:

As a preparation to further configuration, you have to maintain these three users in the SAP S/4HANA client and grant each user the respective authorizations.

Prerequisite

Make sure that scope items 1YB and 1HB are active.

Settings for S/4HANA Public Cloud

1) Create communication user using App "Maintain Communication Users" (App ID F1338).

2) Create two communication systems for communication scenarios SAP_COM_0087 and SAP_COM_0326 and two communication arrangements respectively. The key requirement here is to specify the same communication user in the mentioned artifacts.

2.a) Use App "Communication Systems" (App ID F1762) to create two new systems for each communication scenario.

2.b) Use App "Communication Arrangements" (App ID F1763) to create two respective arrangements.

Note that a new service "Start Jobs to pull Plan Data from SAC" (API_FINPLANPULLJOB) has been included in the communication scenario SAP_COM_0087, that will be used in our integration task.

Note that a generic service "External Scheduler Integration" of comm. scenario SAP_COM_0326 (BC_EXT_APPJOB_MANAGEMENT) service will not be used in our integration task.

After the described configuration is done, your communication user must show up as used in the following communication artifacts:

Once communication arrangements get successfully activated, your communication user acquires all necessary authorizations to complete the desired task. The key authorizations are permission to run service API_FINPLANPULLJOB (inherited from communication scenario SAP_COM _0087) and permission to start application jobs on behalf of another user (inherited from communication scenario SAP_COM _0326).

3) Create a new business role using App “Maintain Business Roles” (App ID F1492). The minimal set of IAM Applications for performing our task include:

IAM App IDPurpose
SAC_INT_PULL_TRANFor running application "Manage Financial Plan Data Jobs for SAP Analytics Cloud Integration"
F7902_TRANFor running application "Schedule Financial Plan Data Jobs for SAP Analytics Cloud Integration"
F1240_TRAN and SP01_SIMPLE_TRAN To display the results of Application Jobs, i.e. application log which was created by another (communication) user

Click on "Maintain Restrictions". Maintain restrictions for restriction type "Activities on Other User’s Jobs" so that application logs for Job Catalog Entry SAP_FINS_INT_SAC_S4 can be viewed only. Specify App Job Part = JOB, SPOOL.

Click "Back" to get back to the main page of the role editor and save.

4) You need a "monitoring" user to view application jobs and application logs. If necessary, create a new business user for this purpose using App "Maintain Business Users" (App ID F1303). Alternatively, you might already have an existing business user in the system. In any of these cases, assign your newly created business role from p. 3 to your "monitoring" user.

5) Specify the "posting" user. You can do this by assigning such user to a Business User Group with pre-defined name ZCB_SAC_PULL using App "Maintain Business User Groups" (App ID F6399).
Note that the "posting" user for starting jobs can be the same as "monitoring" user from p. 4 or they can be different S/4HANA users.

Settings in SAP Analytics Cloud

1) Create a new connection of type HTTP API:

In the next dialog specify Data Service URL in the form:
https://<<s/4hana_tenant>>:443/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_finplanpulljob/srvd_a2x/sap/finplansacpulljob/0001/FinPlanPullJob
Authentication Type = Basic Authentication
User Name = <<communication user name (alias)>>
Password = <<password for communication user>>

2) Go to Multi Actions -> create Multi Action:

Add API Step to your Multi Action:

In the properties of API Step:

  • select HTTP API Connection from p. 1:

  • Enter API URL in the form:

https://<<s/4hana_tenant>>/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_finplanpulljob/srvd_a2x/sap/finplansacpulljob/0001/FinPlanPullJob/SAP__self.ScheduleJob

  • Set tick mark "Require CSRF Token" on.
  • Enter CSRF Token URL in the form:

https://<<s/4hana_tenant>>:443/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_finplanpulljob/srvd_a2x/sap/finplansacpulljob/0001/FinPlanPullJob

  • Enter Body of API request. Note that some of the parameters are optional. Refer to two examples below:
Minimal formExtended form

{
    "PlanDataImportConfigurationID": "<<your_config_ID>>"
}

{
    "PlanDataImportConfigurationID": "<<your_config_ID>>",
    "PlanDataImportIsTestMode": true/false,
    "PlanDataImportJobDelay": <<number_of_seconds>>,
    "PlanDataImportNumberOfAttempts": <<number>>
}

If job delay parameter equals to 0 or omitted, the job starts immediately. However, if you are using SAC subscriptions in your configuration, and amount of changed data in your model is big enough, then calculation of delta may take some time on SAC side. If this is the case, your job, if started immediately, may issue a request to your SAC model too early (i.e. before delta is ready on SAC side) and the corresponding response may return an old state of delta (i.e. may not return some latest changes). With this parameter you can mitigate this problem by starting your job with some delay.
The “number of attempts” parameter is another way to mitigate the risk of long delta calculation. The service keeps sending requests to the SAC model repeatedly several times until the response returns any record. Once the request returns any data, the service stops making attempts.

  • Under Generic API settings -> Response, choose option "Get API trigger status from HTTP status code and response body".
  • Press "Configure fields mapping" to map the fields of the service API_FINPLANPULLJOB with the fields of the API step:

  • In the Fields Mapping popup, go through the three configuration steps:
    • For "1. Enter JSON", copy and paste the following template of response for our service:

{
"PlanDataImportJobIdentifier": "JobID",
"PlanDataImportJobMessageText": "In Process",
"PlanDataImportJobStatusText": "IN_PROCESS"
}

  • For "2. Map Fields", map three fields between response of our service and expected fields of API Step – Job ID, Status and Message:

PlanDataImportJobIdentifier = JobID
PlanDataImportStatusText = Status
PlanDataImportJobMessageText = Message

The result of the mapping must look like below:

  • For "3. Map Status Value", map three values of expected by API Step “Status” field and actual response value of our service:

  • Under Get API Execution Request, choose method “Asynchronous Return”.
  • Enter “Polling API URL” in the form:

https://<<s/4hana_tenant>>:443/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_finplanpulljob/srvd_a2x/sap/finplansacpulljob/0001/FinPlanPullJob/SAP__self.GetJobStatus(PlanDataImportJobIdentifier='${jobId}')

  • Under Get API Execution Result -> Response, choose option "Get API execution result from HTTP status code and response body".
  • Press "Configure fields mapping" to map the fields of the service response with expected fields of the API step:

  • In the Fields Mapping popup, go through three configuration steps:
    • For “1. Enter JSON”, copy and paste the following template of response for our service:

{
"PlanDataImportJobMessageText": "Job Completed with 100 records",
"PlanDataImportJobStatusText": "DONE"
}

  • For "2. Map Fields", map two fields between the response of our service and expected fields of API Step – Status and Message:
    PlanDataImportJobStatusText = Status
    PlanDataImportJobMessageText = Message

The result of the mapping must look like below:

  • For "3. Map Status Value", map the three values of expected by API Step “Status” field and actual response value of our service:

Note: there is a documentation and tutorial for adding an API Step 

3) Incorporate your Multi Action into your SAC Story:

Open SAC Story and choose Insert -> Starters -> Multi Action Starter:

Specify Label, Description and select your Multi Action from p. 2:

4) Save your Story and switch to View mode.

Smoke test

1) Create your Configuration ID using App “Manage Financial Plan Data Jobs - for SAP Analytics Cloud Integration” (App ID SAC_INT_PULL). Here is an example of the configuration we used in this smoke test:

2) Optionally, check that integration works as expected if you trigger it directly from the App “Schedule Financial Plan Data Jobs for SAP Analytics Cloud Integration” (App ID F7902).

3) As far as our configuration has Delta mode, in this smoke test we are going to change a data slice which is given in the filter settings of your Configuration ID. After you've saved your configuration, a new subscription gets automatically created on SAC side, which is immediately starting to monitor all the changes in the defined data slice of your model.

Go to your SAC Story and make any change(s) in the cell(s) inside this data slice.

4) Once you’ve made your changes in your SAC Story, click on Publish Data and Press Multi Action Starter.

During execution of the integration job, you should see a pop-up message on the screen:

Once the job is finished, you may get different messages.
In case of successful integration:

In case of an error at integration, the error message gets propagated directly to the message toast:

An error can be also caused by wrong configuration in S/4HANA or by providing incorrect parameters in the Multi Action:

Note that all messages you get in the form of message toasts are also available in the Job Monitor view:

In addition to high-level messaging in the SAC Job monitor, the planner has also a possibility for more deep analysis of integration flow. It may be necessary, for instance, for analysis of issues/errors. Planner may use the "monitoring" user in S/4HANA to log-in to SAP Fiori Launchpad and read application logs:

Conclusion

With the described approach, the planner can benefit from two powerful features in the SAC Pull framework which complement each other: the so-called "Delta Mode" of integration and the functionality to trigger integration by clicking a "Multi Action Starter" button in SAC Story. The first feature significantly shortens integration times, whereas the second one brings easiness of starting integration. This scenario is particularly useful where a planner modifies model data frequently in SAC Story and, on the other hand, there is a requirement to replicate these changes into S/4HANA on request.

entry.title: Da revisão do forecast à decisão: como coordenar pessoas, versões e tarefas no SAC
entry.content:
Considere um cenário hipotético de fechamento mensal com três unidades. Não há aqui uma implantação real nem resultados medidos. A situação serve para discutir uma distinção prática: trabalhar os números, revisar seu conteúdo e decidir sobre a publicação são responsabilidades que precisam ser explicitadas.

No SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC), recursos de planejamento e colaboração podem apoiar essas atividades. O método proposto é conectá-los sem tratar comentário, tarefa concluída e versão publicada como se fossem a mesma coisa.

1. Defina a revisão antes de distribuir trabalho

Forecast é a previsão usada para acompanhar o planejamento. A revisão precisa começar com uma definição compartilhada:

Qual previsão está em discussão, para qual período, em quais unidades e para apoiar qual decisão?

A recomendação é registrar também qual versão está sendo trabalhada. Sem essa referência, pedir apenas que cada responsável “atualize seus números” não explicita a relação entre a contribuição individual e o cenário em análise.

No exemplo hipotético, a equipe central poderia combinar o recorte da revisão e a versão de trabalho antes de distribuir tarefas. Isso é uma escolha de processo apoiada pela gestão de versões, não uma promessa de que a ferramenta definirá o processo pela organização.

2. Versão privada é espaço de trabalho, não publicação

A gestão de versões permite trabalhar nos próprios dados antes de publicar, explorar cenários e fazer análise de desvios. Também oferece recursos para desfazer e refazer mudanças, consultar histórico e retornar uma versão privada a um estado anterior.

Na revisão proposta, cada responsável poderia usar uma versão privada para testar suas mudanças. O ponto não é produzir cenários sem critério. É preservar a distinção entre uma hipótese em elaboração e os dados que se pretende publicar.

Se a discussão apontar outra direção, o histórico e a possibilidade de retornar a um estado anterior fazem parte desse trabalho. Não é necessário apresentar cada tentativa como a previsão já decidida.

A pergunta de controle, portanto, não deve ser somente “você terminou?”. Deve incluir:

“Qual versão foi revisada e o que ainda precisa ser decidido antes da publicação?”

A resposta precisa estar no processo, não ser presumida a partir de uma tela.

3. Confira o recorte e o que a validação realmente garante

Uma story é o ambiente de relatório e análise do SAC, com tabelas, gráficos e elementos interativos. Ela pode apoiar a conversa sobre os números. Mas a navegação na análise também precisa de contexto.

Bookmarks, por exemplo, guardam filtros e prompts, isto é, parâmetros de seleção. Não são substitutos da versão de dados de planejamento. Para a revisão, recomendo identificar tanto o cenário em trabalho quanto o recorte exibido, sem confundir uma visão salva com uma publicação.

Outra camada são as regras de validação. Elas definem combinações permitidas entre membros de dimensões e impedem operações de planejamento fora dessas combinações.

É uma verificação específica: passar por uma combinação permitida não deve ser apresentado como prova de que uma premissa de negócio foi aprovada.

Há ainda os bloqueios de dados. Eles permitem proteger recortes, delegar responsáveis e restringir a edição aos donos. Mudanças nos bloqueios podem ser programadas no calendário.

Antes de incorporar isso ao fechamento, é preciso verificar a configuração aplicável, em vez de pressupor que todo recorte já está protegido.

4. Dê responsáveis e revisores ao trabalho

O calendário do SAC permite criar tarefas, atribuir pessoas à execução e designar outras para revisar. Processos podem reunir várias tarefas. Também há acompanhamento de status, prazos e lembretes.

No cenário hipotético, essas capacidades podem organizar as contribuições das três unidades e suas revisões.

Para cada tarefa, a recomendação é deixar claro:

  • Executor: quem realiza a atividade.

  • Revisor: quem verifica o trabalho realizado.

  • Prazo: quando a atividade deve ser concluída.

Isso não significa que criar uma tarefa estabeleça automaticamente o vínculo com uma versão privada ou publique seus dados.

O calendário organiza trabalho e acompanhamento; a decisão sobre o conteúdo e sua publicação precisa continuar explícita.

Ao consultar o andamento, a equipe central deve perguntar o que aquele status representa no processo definido.

“Concluído” pode descrever o trabalho atribuído, mas não deve ser usado, por inferência, como declaração de que toda a previsão foi aprovada e publicada.

5. Use o feedback no contexto adequado

Comentários podem ser feitos em uma página da story, em um ponto de dado ou em um widget, que é um elemento da análise. Também é possível mencionar pessoas.

Discussões permitem conversar com usuários e equipes, incluir anexos e relacionar outras stories.

Na revisão hipotética, um revisor poderia registrar uma pergunta sobre a premissa de uma previsão no ponto relevante da análise. A discussão com a equipe poderia reunir a conversa necessária para esclarecer a dúvida.

Não estamos atribuindo valor financeiro nem desfecho a esse exemplo.

O critério é simples:

  • Comentários: localizar dúvidas e observações no contexto da análise.

  • Discussões: facilitar a troca de informações entre pessoas e equipes.

Esses recursos são meios de feedback e colaboração. Não devem ser tratados como aprovação formal só porque alguém respondeu ou foi mencionado.

6. Um fluxo ilustrativo, sem automatismos presumidos

Para a Controladoria do exemplo, o método poderia seguir esta ordem:

 

Etapa 1. Preparar a revisão

Definir previsão, período, unidades e versão de trabalho.

 

Etapa 2. Atribuir contribuições

Indicar executores, revisores e prazos nas tarefas.

Etapa 3. Trabalhar os cenários

Testar mudanças em versões privadas e consultar o histórico quando necessário.

Etapa 4. Conferir o conteúdo

Revisar o recorte na story, registrar dúvidas e verificar regras de validação e bloqueios aplicáveis.

Etapa 5. Decidir sobre a publicação

Identificar quem pode realizá-la e em quais condições.

Etapa 6. Acompanhar o encerramento

Consultar status e pendências sem equiparar conclusão de tarefa a publicação dos dados.

É uma proposta de organização baseada em capacidades descritas, não uma sequência automaticamente executada pelo SAC.

Não se promete que concluir uma etapa valide o mérito econômico da previsão ou dispare a próxima ação.

Também há um limite de acesso: na base consultada, licença BI permite entrada básica em modelos de planejamento e criação de versões privadas; publicação de versões e uso de ferramentas de planejamento exigem licença de planejamento.

Licenças e permissões precisam ser verificadas antes de distribuir responsabilidades.

 

Conclusão

A revisão fica mais bem definida quando versão de trabalho, verificação do dado e responsabilidade das pessoas deixam de ser uma única ideia chamada “finalizar o forecast”.

No seu processo, quem assume explicitamente a responsabilidade pela validação antes de a versão ser publicada?

entry.title: Antes do dashboard: como escolher conexão, dataset e modelo no SAP Analytics Cloud
entry.content:
Esse é um cenário hipotético de Controladoria, não um relato de implantação. Ele ajuda a separar decisões que parecem uma só quando o pedido chega como “precisamos de um dashboard”. No SAP Analytics Cloud, ou SAC, escolher a base analítica envolve conexão, estrutura dos dados e finalidade de uso. A visualização vem depois dessas escolhas.

Comece pelo que precisa ser entendido

No exemplo, “despesas por centro de custo” ainda deixa espaço para esclarecer o recorte. A equipe quer investigar uma dúvida pontual ou estabelecer uma análise governada? Precisa apenas consultar valores ou também trabalhar com números de planejamento?

Essas perguntas têm correspondência na estrutura analítica. Dimensões são categorias que dão perspectiva aos números, como centro de custo e data. Medidas são os valores numéricos analisados. Um modelo reúne dimensões e medidas para representar um conjunto específico de dados.

Por isso, antes de escolher a apresentação, vale escrever a pergunta com seu contexto: qual valor será observado, por quais categorias e para qual finalidade? No cenário hipotético, essa descrição não precisa antecipar a resposta. Precisa deixar claro o que a equipe pretende analisar.

Conexão é uma decisão com restrições

A conexão permite a comunicação entre o SAC e uma fonte de dados, que pode estar na nuvem ou em ambiente local. Ela é específica para a fonte: trabalhar com diferentes origens exige considerar suas respectivas conexões.

Há dois tipos descritos para esse acesso: live e importação. A escolha não deve começar pela preferência por um nome. Os critérios incluem necessidades funcionais, restrições de privacidade e volume de dados. Também é necessário verificar requisitos técnicos e suporte para a versão e o tipo de conexão utilizados.

Para a Controladoria do exemplo, a recomendação é transformar esses critérios em perguntas à equipe responsável pela fonte. O acesso pretendido é suportado? As exigências de privacidade estão contempladas? Há restrições de volume ou funcionalidades que precisam ser consideradas?

Sem essas respostas, não cabe prometer que qualquer origem atenderá a qualquer desenho. Tampouco cabe declarar live ou importação como solução superior em todos os casos. A decisão precisa corresponder ao ambiente efetivo da organização.

Dataset ou modelo: escolha pela finalidade

Um dataset é uma coleção simples de dados, normalmente organizada em tabela, que pode servir de base para uma story. Story é o nome usado no SAC para esse objeto de análise. Dataset e modelo podem sustentá-lo, mas atendem a necessidades diferentes.

Datasets se destinam a análises simples e ad hoc: explorações pontuais, sem a mesma proposta de governança dos modelos. Modelos são indicados quando a análise exige uma base mais governada ou envolve planejamento. Não se trata de escolher o objeto “mais sofisticado”, e sim aquele coerente com o uso.

No cenário hipotético, uma investigação pontual de despesas pode ser discutida como exploração. Se o objetivo for uma análise governada, a conversa passa a ser sobre modelo. A recorrência do pedido deve motivar essa discussão, mas não substitui a definição do nível de governança necessário.

Há ainda uma separação importante: modelos analíticos são de leitura; modelos de planejamento permitem leitura e escrita. Estes requerem as dimensões Data e Versão, e a escrita depende de permissões de planejamento. Datasets não suportam casos de planejamento.

Logo, se o pedido evoluir de “entender despesas” para “trabalhar uma previsão”, não convém tratar essa mudança apenas como inclusão de uma coluna no painel. A finalidade precisa ser reavaliada à luz do modelo adequado e das permissões envolvidas.

Um exemplo concreto, com fronteiras claras

Um caso documentado de modelo live utiliza SAP HANA em ambiente local. O procedimento seleciona uma visão de cálculo, define a data do pedido como dimensão temporal e visualiza os dados no Data Analyzer.

O exemplo mostra uma combinação específica entre origem, conexão, estrutura e análise. Não demonstra que a fonte de despesas do cenário hipotético está disponível, nem autoriza generalizar o mesmo caminho para todas as origens.

Na criação do modelo live, o tipo de sistema, a conexão e a fonte precisam corresponder à organização. Esse é o ponto aproveitável para a decisão de negócio: pedir a validação da combinação real, em vez de transformar um exemplo técnico em promessa de compatibilidade.

Explore o recorte antes de fechar o desenho

O Data Analyzer é uma aplicação pronta para análise ad hoc. Ele permite trabalhar com visualização em tabela ou gráfico, aplicar filtros e adicionar ou remover dimensões e medidas. Também permite salvar o estado de detalhamento e a análise como um insight.

Na aplicação hipotética, depois de confirmar uma fonte suportada, a equipe poderia testar o recorte de despesas por centro de custo e observar os detalhes necessários. O objetivo dessa etapa seria esclarecer a análise desejada, não afirmar que um resultado financeiro já foi obtido.

Ao salvar o insight, é possível informar nome e descrição. Isso oferece uma forma de guardar o recorte explorado para a discussão sobre o que se deseja visualizar.

Há uma fronteira que merece ficar explícita: medidas calculadas criadas nessa análise existem apenas no insight e não são transferidas para a fonte de dados. Se a equipe usar um cálculo exploratório, precisa tratá-lo como tal, sem apresentá-lo como alteração na origem.

Um checklist antes de solicitar a story

Para conduzir a conversa, proponho cinco verificações:

  • Escrever a pergunta e identificar medidas e dimensões relevantes.

  • Confirmar fonte, suporte da conexão, privacidade, volume e requisitos técnicos.

  • Distinguir exploração pontual de análise governada.

  • Verificar se haverá planejamento e, nesse caso, qual modelo e quais permissões são necessários.

  • Explorar um recorte no Data Analyzer, quando aplicável, e registrar o insight sem confundir cálculo local com mudança na fonte.

Esse roteiro organiza critérios; não dispensa a validação de suporte e configuração no ambiente utilizado. O dashboard é uma forma de apresentar a análise, não uma resposta automática às decisões sobre sua base.

Antes de discutir qual gráfico usar, qual critério pesa mais na sua escolha: a restrição da fonte, a governança da análise ou a necessidade de planejamento?
